title: Functors and Applicatives (COMP40009, Lecture 14)
slides_text: Type constructors and kinds. Int :: *. Maybe :: * -> *. Either :: * -> * -> *. A type constructor needs type arguments before it becomes a type.
The Functor class. class Functor f where fmap :: (a -> b) -> f a -> f b. f must have kind * -> *.
Functor laws. Identity: fmap id = id. Composition: fmap (g . h) = fmap g . fmap h. Laws mean fmap preserves structure.
Applicative. class Functor f => Applicative f where pure :: a -> f a; (<*>) :: f (a -> b) -> f a -> f b. Apply a wrapped function to a wrapped value.

chunks.text: Right, let's get going. Before we can talk about functors we need to be precise about something we've been glossing over, which is the difference between a type and a type constructor.
Int is a type. Bool is a type. You can have a value of type Int. But Maybe on its own is not a type. There is no value whose type is just Maybe.
Maybe is a type constructor. You have to give it a type argument before you get a real type. Maybe Int is a type, Maybe Bool is a type, but Maybe by itself is waiting for an argument.

We describe this with kinds. Kinds are the types of types. Int has kind star. Maybe has kind star to star, because it takes one type and gives you back a type. Either has kind star to star to star, it needs two.
Hold on to that, because it matters right now. Here is the Functor type class. class Functor f where fmap has type a to b, to f a, to f b.
Look at where f appears: f a and f b. So f is applied to a type. That means f must be a type constructor of kind star to star. That is why Maybe can be a Functor but Int cannot.

So what does fmap do? It takes an ordinary function from a to b and lifts it to work inside the structure. For lists, fmap is just map. It applies the function to every element and leaves the structure alone.
For Maybe, fmap applies the function if there is a Just, and if you have Nothing you get Nothing back. Same idea: change the values inside, never the shape around them.
Now, I keep saying never the shape. That is not just a convention, it is enforced by the functor laws. Every lawful Functor instance has to satisfy two equations.
The first is the identity law: fmap id equals id. If you map the identity function over a structure, you must get exactly the same structure back. Same length list, same Just or Nothing.
The second is the composition law: fmap of g composed with h equals fmap g composed with fmap h. Mapping twice is the same as mapping once with the composed function.

Together these laws mean fmap preserves structure. An fmap that reversed the list, or dropped the first element, would break the identity law, so it is not a valid functor instance, even if it type checks.
OK. Functors have a limitation. fmap takes a plain function. But what if the function itself is inside the structure? What if you have Just of plus three and Just of four?

That is what Applicative is for. Applicative is a subclass of Functor with two operations: pure, which takes a value and wraps it in a minimal structure, and the apply operator, written angle star angle.
Apply has type f of a to b, to f a, to f b. It applies a wrapped function to a wrapped value. So Just plus three apply Just four gives Just seven, and if either side is Nothing you get Nothing.

And notice f has to be a type constructor again, star to star, which is why every Applicative must first be a Functor. That is enough for today, next time we will see why this lets us combine independent effects.
